statement.excerpt: People will argue that AI is “really helpful with research,” despite the fact that any research you receive from AI will absolutely have hallucinations

from_speaker: any research you receive from AI
our_interpretation: Read as a universal claim about substantive research responses, not merely a warning that hallucinations are possible.
A hallucination is a fabricated or false factual assertion, including a falsely attributed citation.
Use January–March 2026, the latest completed quarter before the post, for the ongoing description of AI research tools.
A correct isolated answer or citation is insufficient unless the entire substantive research response was checked.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence establishes that every substantive AI research response within the relevant scope contains at least one hallucination. A high average error rate alone is insufficient.
criteria.contradiction_condition: At least one substantive research response generated in the target period is independently checked in full and contains no hallucinations.

evidence.explanation: The study documents reliability problems across six research agents on deliberately hallucination-prone tasks. Its aggregate trajectory measures do not establish that every final research response contains a false assertion.

This contradicts an unrestricted suggestion that AI cannot answer factual questions correctly. However, correctness on the specified clinical question is not evidence that every assertion in a substantial research response was checked, and the retrieved passage does not establish generation dates.

The researchers define accurate responses as correct and grounded, providing strong counterevidence to an unrestricted universal claim. The manuscript dates the relevant evaluation to April 2024, outside the selected period; its retrieved text identifies an August 2026 revision.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A dated research response from the target period, together with an independent check of all substantive assertions and citations.
